en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Village of Bhūta 17.
The Training Rule on Expulsion At that time,
the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of seventeen monks were repairing a certain remote large monastery,
thinking, "We shall spend the rains retreat here.
The group of six monks saw the group of seventeen monks repairing the monastery.
Having seen them, they said this:
"Friends, these seventeen monks from the group of seventeen are repairing the monastery.
Come, let us rouse them."
Some said, “Wait, friends, until they have repaired it; once it has been repaired, we will raise him up.
Then the group-of-six monks said this to the group-of-seventeen monks:
“Get up, friend; our monastery has come into view.
“Shouldn’t you have informed us beforehand, friend, so that we might have prepared something else?
“But isn’t this a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha, friend?”
“It belongs to the Saṅgha, friend.
“Get up, friend; our monastery has come to us.
“The monastery is large, friend.”
“You too may dwell here; we too shall dwell here.
“Get up, friends! Our monastery has been reached,” they said, and being angry and displeased, they seized them by the neck and dragged them out.
As they were being dragged out, they wept.
The monks said, "Friends, why are you weeping?
"Friends, these monks of the group of six, angry and displeased, are throwing us out from our dwellings belonging to the Saṅgha.
Those monks who were few in desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.
“How indeed can the group-of-six monks, being angry and displeased, eject monks from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you, being angry and displeased, ejected monks from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How, you foolish men, can you, being angry and displeased, eject monks from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk, being angry and displeased, should himself eject or cause another to eject a monk from a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whoever" means whoever such as this...
"a monk."
...pe... this is the meaning intended here by the term "bhikkhu.
A "bhikkhunī" is one other than a bhikkhu.
"Purchased and displeased" means dissatisfied,
with a troubled mind, having become resentful.
"Belonging to the Sangha" refers to a monastery.
"It has been given to the Saṅgha and relinquished.
"Should expel" means:
having seized her by the arm, she drags her out to the entrance; there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Having seized [her] by the face, he drags her outside: there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Even if he causes her to pass through many doors with a single effort, there is an offense of expiation.
"He should have her dragged out" means...
If she commands another, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If, having been commanded once, she causes [the person] to pass through many doors, there is an offense of expiation.
If, being angry and displeased, she ejects or causes to be ejected from a dwelling belonging to the Sangha while perceiving it as belonging to the Sangha, there is an offense of expiation.
If one, being angry and displeased, ejects or causes another to eject [an item] belonging to the Saṅgha while being in doubt [about its ownership], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one, being angry and displeased, ejects or causes another to eject [an item] belonging to the Saṅgha while perceiving it as belonging to an individual, there is an offense of expiation.
If one ejects or causes another to eject that person’s personal requisites, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one drags out, or causes to be dragged out, [a person] from a monastery, or from the vicinity of a monastery, or from a reception hall, or from a pavilion, or from the foot of a tree, or from an open space, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one drags out, or causes to be dragged out, that person’s requisites, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

If one drags out, or causes to be dragged out, a person who is not fully ordained from a monastery, or from the vicinity of a monastery, or from a reception hall, or from a pavilion, or from the foot of a tree, or from an open space, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he throws out his requisites or causes them to be thrown out, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it belongs to an individual and he perceives it as belonging to the Saṅgha, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it belongs to an individual and he is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it belongs to another individual and he perceives it as belonging to another individual, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it belongs to himself, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If one ejects one who is shameless, or causes him to be ejected;
if one ejects his requisites, or causes them to be ejected;
or if one ejects one who is insane, or causes him to be ejected.
If one drags out or causes to be dragged out the requisites of one who creates quarrels,
who creates strife, who creates disputes, who creates contention, or who creates legal issues in the Saṅgha;
or if one drags out or causes to be dragged out his requisites.
If one ejects, or causes to be ejected, a resident pupil or a co-resident student who is not conducting himself properly;
or if one ejects, or causes to be ejected, his requisites;
or if one is insane.
"For one who is a first offender":
the seventh training rule concerning expulsion is finished.
